title: Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento
goal: By the end you can explain the expression problem and replace a Visitor with a sealed switch, write a lazy paging iterator with Kotlin's `sequence {}` (and know what Java needs instead), take snapshots that don't leak with Memento, and say when a Mediator helps.

warmup.q: A codebase evaluates expressions with a classic Visitor: `ExprVisitor` with `visitNum`, `visitAdd`, `visitMul`, and four visitor classes. You add a fifth node type, `Neg`. What do you have to touch?
options: Only the new `Neg` class
The visitor interface, an `accept` on `Neg`, and all four visitor classes
Only the visitor interface
Nothing: the visitor finds `Neg` through reflection
warmup.why: Visitor makes new operations cheap (a new visitor class) and new cases expensive: every visitor must learn the new case, and the interface needs a `visitNeg`. That is one half of the expression problem. A sealed type with `switch` has the same trade-off, but the compiler lists every place to change.

sections.h: Visitor, the expression problem, and sealed types

try.title: Add a case in both styles
steps: Run `VisitorVsSwitch` (Java or Kotlin) and check both results agree.

Add a `Neg` case. Java: add `Neg` to `permits` and `record Neg(Expr e) implements Expr { public <R> R accept(ExprVisitor<R> v) { return v.visitNeg(this); } }`. Kotlin: `data class Neg(val e: Expr) : Expr { override fun <R> accept(v: ExprVisitor<R>) = v.visitNeg(this) }`. Build with the demo command.
Fix each error the compiler gives you, build again, and keep a count of the places you edited.

try.expect: Both print `(2 + 3 * 4) = 14` from the visitor and from the switch, then `0 * (2 + 3 * 4) = 0`. Kotlin lists all three errors at once: `unresolved reference 'visitNeg'` and `'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'is Neg' branch` twice. javac reports them in rounds: `cannot find symbol` first; add `visitNeg` to `ExprVisitor` and you get `Eval is not abstract and does not override abstract method visitNeg(Neg)`; implement that and the two switches fail with `does not cover all possible input values`. Visitor style cost the interface, `accept` and every visitor; switch style cost one branch per function.

figure.caption: Without a mediator every service knows the others. With one, each knows only the hub, and the coordination rules live in one place.

analogy: A visitor is a tax inspector who visits every kind of business with a different checklist for each; a new kind of business means every inspector learns a new checklist. An iterator is a librarian fetching books one at a time from the stacks, so you can start reading before the last shelf is reached. A memento is a photo of a whiteboard before you erase it. A mediator is an air-traffic tower: planes talk to the tower, never to each other. The analogy breaks on the photo. A photo can't change after you take it, but a software memento that shares a list with the live object changes every time you edit, which is the bug the lesson's demo shows.
in_your_world: The PSP clients in your services almost certainly page: refunds, disputes, payouts, settlement lines. Expose each as a Kotlin `Sequence` (or a Java `Iterator`) that fetches lazily, and the reconciliation job can stop at the first mismatch without downloading the rest. Mind that iterating twice hits the API twice. Memento is how a back-office tool offers undo on a draft refund batch, and how an event-sourced ledger keeps snapshots so that replay stays fast. Mediator is your checkout orchestration: inside one Quarkus service it can be a small router or a shared flow, and across services it is the Temporal workflow that sequences inventory, payment and shipping activities. Visitor shows up mostly when you write annotation processors or bytecode tools; in your own domain code, sealed types and `switch` or `when` replace it.
mistake: The most common Memento mistake is a shallow snapshot: `save()` stores a reference to the object's live mutable list (or an array, or a mutable nested object) instead of a copy. It happens because records and data classes look immutable, so `new State(items, coupon)` feels like a snapshot. It isn't: the record holds the same list the object keeps editing, so the "saved" state changes with every edit, and undo restores the present instead of the past. Copy every mutable part when you save (`List.copyOf`, `toList()`), copy again when you restore, and test it the way the lab does: save, edit, restore, edit again, restore again.

compare.title: Replacing a visitor: nested patterns in Java, guards in Kotlin

java.title: Expr.java

kotlin.title: Expr.kt
kotlin.src:
sealed interface Expr
data class Num(val value: Int) : Expr
data class Add(val left: Expr, val right: Expr) : Expr
data class Mul(val left: Expr, val right: Expr) : Expr

fun eval(e: Expr): Int = when (e) {
    is Num -> e.value
    is Add -> eval(e.left) + eval(e.right)
    is Mul if e.left == Num(0) -> 0                         // no nested patterns in Kotlin: a guard says it
    is Mul -> eval(e.left) * eval(e.right)
}

fun show(e: Expr): String = when (e) {                      // a new operation: one new function, no class touched
    is Num -> e.value.toString()
    is Add -> "(${show(e.left)} + ${show(e.right)})"
    is Mul -> "${show(e.left)} * ${show(e.right)}"
}

compare.note: Both delete the visitor interface and every `accept` method, and both make a new operation a single function. The difference is how far the patterns reach. Java 21 record patterns nest, so `Mul(Num(var z), var r) when z == 0` matches "a multiplication whose left side is the literal 0" in one case, and binds the fields as it goes. Kotlin's `when` matches on type and smart-casts, but has no destructuring patterns, so the same rule is a guard (`is Mul if e.left == Num(0)`), which works because data classes compare by value. Guards in `when` are stable since Kotlin 2.2.0. In both, adding a case such as `Neg` breaks every function that switches over `Expr`, which is the compiler listing your work.

worked.title: Retire a visitor in four steps

steps.say: A fee-formula engine evaluates and prints expressions with a classic visitor. Product wants negation. Before reading on, list every file a `Neg` node touches in this design.

`Neg` needs a `visitNeg` on the interface, an `accept` on itself, and a new method in `Eval`, `Show` and every other visitor. The hierarchy is closed and ours, so retire the machinery first: drop `accept` and the interface, and write each operation as a switch. Behavior doesn't change; run the old tests.
steps.alt_code:
sealed interface Expr                                          // 1. no accept, no visitor interface
data class Num(val value: Int) : Expr
data class Add(val left: Expr, val right: Expr) : Expr
data class Mul(val left: Expr, val right: Expr) : Expr

fun eval(e: Expr): Int = when (e) {                            // 2. each visitor becomes one function
    is Num -> e.value
    is Add -> eval(e.left) + eval(e.right)
    is Mul -> eval(e.left) * eval(e.right)
}

steps.say: Now add the case, and compile before writing any logic. The errors are the to-do list: one per function that switches over `Expr`.
Fill in one branch per function. A brand-new operation, counting nodes for a complexity limit, is one more function, and no type changes at all.
steps.alt_code:
is Neg -> -eval(e.e)                                           // 4. in eval
is Neg -> "-${show(e.e)}"                                      //    in show

fun count(e: Expr): Int = when (e) {                           // 5. a new operation: one function
    is Num -> 1
    is Add -> 1 + count(e.left) + count(e.right)
    is Mul -> 1 + count(e.left) + count(e.right)
    is Neg -> 1 + count(e.e)
}

lab.title: A lazy paging sequence and an invoice draft with undo
steps: Run the tests once: all nine fail.
In `Paging.kt`, write `pagedSequence` with the `sequence {}` builder: start at cursor 0, fetch a page, hand out its items, follow `next` until it is null.

In `InvoiceDraft`, add a private data class that implements `Memento` and holds the lines and the note. `save()` stores copies; `restore` checks the type with `require`, then copies the lines back into the draft's own list.
Write `DraftHistory`: keep mementos in an `ArrayDeque`, drop the oldest when there are more than `limit`, and restore the newest on `undo`.
Run the tests until all nine pass. Then read the test that restores the same memento twice, and say which line of your `restore` makes it pass.
hints: Inside `sequence {}`, an ordinary `while` loop and `yieldAll(page.items)` are all you need. An empty page yields nothing, and the loop carries on to the next cursor.
After `require(m is State) { "..." }`, Kotlin smart-casts `m` to `State` for the rest of the function. A private nested class may implement a public nested interface.
In `restore`, `lines.clear()` then `lines.addAll(m.lines)` keeps the memento's list untouched. Assigning the memento's list to the draft instead would let the next edit change the memento.

drill.title: A paging iterator in Java, from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write the Java version: `static Iterator<String> refunds(Function<Integer, RefundPage> fetch)`, where `RefundPage(List<String> items, Integer next)` and `next` is null on the last page. It must skip empty pages and fetch nothing until `hasNext` is called. Then write the Kotlin `sequence {}` version and compare how much state each one keeps.

alt.title: Kotlin

recap: The expression problem: virtual methods make new cases cheap, Visitor makes new operations cheap. Sealed types plus `switch` or `when` give Visitor's side with no `accept` and no visitor interface.
Delete visitors for closed hierarchies you own. Keep Visitor for open hierarchies or library APIs, such as annotation processing and bytecode tools.
Kotlin's `sequence {}` turns a plain loop into a lazy iterator. Java needs a hand-written `Iterator`, with `while`, not `if`, in `hasNext`.
A built sequence is cold (iterating again reruns the block) and may stop early, so `finally` inside it may never run.
Memento: save a private, immutable snapshot that copies every mutable part, restore by copying back in, and bound the history.
Mediator: colleagues talk only to a hub that holds the coordination rules. Keep it to routing and sequencing.

quiz.q: Your team owns a sealed `PaymentInstruction` hierarchy with five records, and keeps adding operations: validate, render, price, export. Which design makes each new operation cheapest?
options: A classic Visitor with an `accept` method on each record
An abstract method per operation on the sealed interface
One function per operation with an exhaustive `switch` or `when`
`instanceof` chains with a final `else` that throws
quiz.why: Operations are the axis that grows, so you want operations to be single functions: a sealed switch gives that, with the compiler checking each one covers all five records. A Visitor gets the same trade-off with more machinery. Abstract methods make each new operation touch all five records, and an `instanceof` chain loses the compiler's check.

quiz.q: A Java paging iterator has `if (!current.hasNext() && cursor != null)` in `hasNext`. Pages are `[rf_1, rf_2]`, then an empty page, then `[rf_3]`. What does a full iteration return?
options: It throws `NoSuchElementException`
It loops forever
quiz.why: After `rf_2`, `hasNext` fetches the empty page once, finds nothing, and returns false, because `if` doesn't try again. The iteration ends early and `rf_3` is never seen, with no error. `while` keeps fetching until it finds an item or runs out of pages.

quiz.q: `val refunds = pagedSequence(fetch)` uses the `sequence {}` builder. The code calls `refunds.count()` and then `refunds.first()`. How many times is page 0 fetched?
options: Once: a sequence caches its pages
Twice: each terminal operation runs the block again from the top
Never: sequences are lazy
Once, but only if the pages are small
quiz.why: A sequence from `sequence {}` is cold: every new iteration starts the block over. `count()` walks all pages and `first()` starts again from page 0. If you need the items twice, collect them once with `toList()`, or accept the second round of API calls.

quiz.q: `Draft.save()` returns `new State(lines, note)`, where `lines` is the draft's own `ArrayList`. The analyst saves, adds a line, and restores. What do they get?
options: The draft as it was at save time
An `UnsupportedOperationException`
A `ConcurrentModificationException`
The draft with the new line still in it, because the snapshot shares the live list
quiz.why: The record holds a reference to the same list the draft keeps editing, so the new line is in the "saved" state too. Depending on how `restore` copies, you get the present back or even an empty list. Copy every mutable part on save (`List.copyOf`) and on restore.

quiz.q: From *Observer and Command*: an analyst's draft supports undo for "add line" and for "apply discount rules", which has no simple inverse. Which approach handles both?
options: A command stack where every command implements `undo()`
A memento saved before each edit, restored on undo
A StateFlow of the draft that collectors can rewind
A Chain of Responsibility of undo handlers
quiz.why: Command-based undo needs an inverse for every command, and "apply discount rules" doesn't have a clean one. A snapshot taken before any edit can always be restored, whatever the edit did. The two combine well: commands for the log, mementos for the undo. A StateFlow keeps only the latest value, so there is nothing to rewind to.

flashcards.front: What is the expression problem, in one line each?
flashcards.back: Virtual methods: new cases are cheap, new operations touch every class. Visitor (or sealed + switch): new operations are cheap, new cases touch every operation.

flashcards.front: When does Visitor still fit in modern Java or Kotlin?
flashcards.back: For open hierarchies across modules, or when a library hands you one: `ElementVisitor` in annotation processors, javac's Tree API, ASM's `ClassVisitor`.

flashcards.front: Java pattern for "a multiplication whose left side is 0"? And Kotlin?
flashcards.back: Java 21: `case Mul(Num(var z), var r) when z == 0`. Kotlin: `is Mul if e.left == Num(0)` (no nested patterns).

flashcards.front: Why `while`, not `if`, in a paging iterator's `hasNext`?
flashcards.back: An empty page must not end the iteration; `while` keeps fetching until it finds an item or runs out of pages.

flashcards.front: Iterating a `sequence {}` twice: what happens to the work inside it?
flashcards.back: It runs again from the top: sequences built that way are cold. Collect with `toList()` if you need the items twice.

flashcards.front: Why can `finally` inside `sequence {}` or `iterator {}` fail to run?
flashcards.back: If the consumer stops early, the rest of the block never runs. Open resources at the call site with `use {}`.
It copies every mutable part on save, restore copies back in, only the originator can read it, and the history is bounded.

terms.plain: One class per operation, with a method per case, called through `accept` on each element.
Choosing code by two runtime types: `accept` picks the case, `visit` picks the operation.
No plain design makes both new cases and new operations cheap; you pick the axis that grows.
An object that hands out a collection's elements one at a time without exposing how they are stored.
A sequence whose work reruns for every iteration, from the start.
An opaque snapshot of an object's state that only the object can read and restore.
A hub that holds the rules for how several parts react to each other, so they don't call each other.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate wants to add a Visitor to the sealed `PaymentInstruction` hierarchy "so we can add operations without touching the classes". Explain what you would do instead, and when you would agree with them.
explain_back.answer: We own the hierarchy and it's sealed, so we already get what a visitor gives: we can add an operation without touching the records by writing one function with a `switch` (or `when`) over the five types. The compiler checks that each function covers every type, and record patterns let us match nested shapes that a visitor can't express easily. A visitor would add an interface with five methods and an `accept` on every record, and nothing else. The cost is the same either way when a new instruction type arrives: every operation must handle it, but with sealed types the compiler lists each one. I'd agree to a visitor if the hierarchy were open to other modules we can't recompile, or if we were plugging into a library that already speaks visitors, such as an annotation processor.

deeper.body:
Kotlin's `sequence {}` is built on the same machinery as coroutines, but restricted. Its block runs on a `SequenceScope`, which allows only `yield` and `yieldAll` to suspend, so you can't call `delay` or another suspend function inside it. For asynchronous paging, where each page fetch is itself a suspending HTTP call, use `flow {}` and `emit` instead: a `Flow` is the suspending cousin of a sequence, cold in the same way, and covered in the coroutines track.

Java's `Iterator` has an optional `remove()`, and its Javadoc says iterators "allow the caller to remove elements from the underlying collection during the iteration with well-defined semantics". That's why `iterator.remove()` is safe inside a loop where `list.remove(x)` throws `ConcurrentModificationException`. For paging iterators, leave `remove()` unsupported, which is the default.

Visitor and Composite often travel together: a visitor walks a composite tree. With sealed types, the walk is just recursion in each function, as in *Composite, Bridge and Flyweight*. If trees get deep enough to overflow the stack, an explicit stack in an iterator (or a `sequence {}` that pushes children) turns the recursion into iteration.

Memento meets event sourcing in snapshots. An aggregate's state is the fold of its events. Replaying ten thousand events on every load is slow, so the store keeps a snapshot every few hundred events, and loading means restoring the newest snapshot and replaying what came after it. The snapshot format then becomes a contract between versions of your code, so give it a version field from the start.
